title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of photos of migrant workers' daily lives
dek: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on photographing its everyday — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the giant factory really did disappear, only a very few people had kept this archive.
why: Not industry analysis: a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content people interested in the shift in manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta factory era disappeared.
skip: The show promo and event notices at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value unimportant
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process so that manufacturing output is more stable and the people are more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean: anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. There were no machines yet to replace them, but a person's value was already almost unimportant. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system that deliberately flattens individual difference, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train was like riding into a bandits' den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed a window with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. More than thirty hours without being able to sit or drink water; after getting off, his belly was terribly swollen. At Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold as a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan and said it was for Dongguan, then on the expressway they demanded another ten for the toll, and if you didn't pay someone would come up and slap you, and in the end they dumped you in a wasteland with nothing around and made you change vehicles. He says he used the term for so many years and only understood what it meant last year.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 it was very hard to find work; men had a far harder time than women, and factory hiring notices stated outright that they only took female workers aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring notice by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people began to drop, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was left. The captain said you're bragging, go on then, and he did 102. After he got up they had him fight someone; the other man did a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, well, if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — in that era an enormous drain for him. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employees in tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a matter of technique, of getting it sharp. Later he read Chinese photography magazines and found there was so much learning in photography, and that he had no standard by which to judge, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: A model-contest photo passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete it
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding model contests; the workers went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms they had made, and there was pole dancing. In 2008 he changed position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience behind — and sent it to Tencent in time; it went up on the portal and got tens of millions of clicks in a morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss, a lover for the factory manager; the framing was distorted, the boss came under huge pressure and told him to delete it. Tencent said they could only hide it, that they couldn't stop other sites from spreading it virally, and in the end served him a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
points.body: On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he went into the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allows four minutes' rest after two hours; the place where they changed work clothes was hung all over with unused clean-room suits, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow native heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the experience people in photography had told him was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is not a good photo’, so he never used this one. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and it was unexpectedly used as the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he admitted it had its own pull — different readers will have different inner responses to it, so a photographer should interpret his photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories' information was separate, there was no networked computer system, and the social security system didn't require contributions, so this set of papers was lent to many people and got into many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system wouldn't accept it — same ID number, same name, same registered household address — and the enterprises decided you were dishonest and zeroed out your years of service. He says this won't do: our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those years of service are real. When even present-day life has no security, it is simply impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years off.

points.h: Density: he shot for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the theme of the dense life of migrant work, and won the excellence award and the Alpa prize at the third Yingjishi Image Awards. Workers' rallies shot from high up, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung all over with clothes, from a distance airtight; workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual sense of density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting every day with his phone, shooting security training, shooting any fellow worker he happened to see on the road, accumulating day by day, on and off for almost 20 years. When there were so many factories and so much of an era, he had not observed it that way; then one morning he found it so terrifying that even a switch looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as the warp, space as the weft: a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The complete thread he worked out was: time as the warp, space as the weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, and capital's impact on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a composite three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text and objects. Later he changed method: starting from the keyword dagong (working for others), he looked up ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, got 322, went into Baidu Images and began screenshotting all of them — this is the internet's understanding of dagong, to be presented together with his own understanding from actually shooting, in one huge exhibition space. He says this is us viewing the era inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compares himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers who get the credit are carried by Sherpas, so I'll just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets being transported; later it meant being cheated by middlemen and drivers who piled on charges along the way to work.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally known photography agency; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers on its website one by one.
A photography award organised by Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China; Zhan Youbing submitted to it and had his image shown as the lead.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it wasn't about riding a train — you felt like you'd got into a bandits' den.
This is the era: we view the era inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we reach will certainly not be poor; but if we can see a society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
